faq.q: What is an AI Facebook UGC ad?
faq.a: It is a Facebook clip that looks like someone showing your product. An AI avatar holds the pale-blue bottle and a voice explains the pour. You did not book a creator or a studio to film that shot.

faq.q: Does this kind of ad work on Facebook?
faq.a: A clip of a hand pouring the pale-blue bottle sits among posts from friends more naturally than a glossy brand film. Make one opening for gift buyers and another for people replacing a worn bottle, then keep the opening you want to spend on.

faq.q: Can I stop paying a creator for every Facebook test?
faq.a: Yes. Each test comes out of your plan. You are not waiting on a new invoice before the next bottle opening.

faq.q: Do these videos follow Facebook's ad rules?
faq.a: Yes, when the offer is true and the bottle is the one you ship. Publish only after you read Facebook's rules that day. Do not invent a buyer, and do not claim a result you have not seen. We do not submit the ad for you.

faq.q: Will people know the ad is made by AI?
faq.a: Some will, and some will not. The clip is built to feel like a creator video of the bottle. Say it is AI when Facebook asks you to. Do not treat hiding that as the goal.

faq.q: How fast can I get a Facebook ad file?
faq.a: You download the file when the render ends. Pick an avatar, rewrite the first line about the bottle, and you are not holding the launch for a camera crew.

faq.q: What does a Facebook video cost in credits?
faq.a: A video spends 24, 40, 60, or 120 credits for 6, 10, 15, or 30 seconds. A photo spends 24. Starter is $24.50 a month for 200 credits, Pro is $35 for 300, and Premium is $63 for 600. You see the cost before you start. A failed job returns those credits.

faq.q: Where should the price and the offer line go?
faq.a: Put the price and the offer line off the bottle, where the player buttons will not cover them. You add that text in the editor after download.

benefits_h2: Why Sellers Switch to Facebook Video Ads

benefits.d: More of the Facebook budget can buy reach, because a new bottle clip costs less to make than hiring a creator for every test.
When the offer changes, you make a new Facebook video that shows the pale-blue bottle and names the new date. You are not stuck waiting on a creator who is booked out.
When people flick past the opening, you can swap in a hand pouring the bottle. The Facebook video gets another look without a new shoot.

steps_h2: Steps to Make Facebook Ads That Look Customer-Made
steps_lead: You leave with a Facebook video of the bottle that Ads Manager can take.

more_sections.h2: Why a Moving Facebook Ad Wins
more_sections.lead: A moving ad of the serum is harder to scroll past than a still of the same dropper.

items.t: Show the Serum in a Hand
items.d: A clip of a hand holding the serum dropper is harder to pass than a still of that same dropper. The buyer sees it the way a friend would hold it up.

Money that used to pay a creator and a half-day studio for one Facebook video can stay in the ad account. Each serum clip shows its credit charge before it starts, so you can make another opening when the offer changes.

items.t: Match the Line to the Buyer
items.d: You can show the same serum to different buyers, with a different spoken line for each. Put more of the budget on the line you want to spend on, and keep the others for people who already visited the page.

benefits_lead: Your next Facebook video of the pale-blue bottle does not start with a talent email.

reasons.h2: Why Use This for Facebook Ads
reasons.lead: One marketer can cover the bottle offer in more than one language.

items.d: The bottle clip is ready when the offer is ready, so you do not pause the campaign for a creator's other clients.
Several bottle colors can go out as separate files. The files share one feed-shaped template, and the last color is framed as carefully as the first.
You can deliver the Facebook ad in the buyer's language, with the phrasing a local shop would use for the bottle. That version does not need a second crew.
